sentences.text: This fish grew to a length of approximately 1.2 meters.
Its body was flattened when viewed from the front but circular from the side, featuring very large eyes.
The animal possessed round teeth packed closely together, suggesting it likely fed on coral and shellfish.
The earliest definite fossil record comes from the Middle Jurassic (Bajocian) of Scotland, originally assigned to the species G. goweri.
Researchers believe Gyrodus may have possessed a sickle-shaped dorsal fin that allowed it to swim at high speeds in open ocean.
Dental microwear evidence indicates that Gyrodus planidens closed its jaw using a propalinal motion where the prearticular sheared against the vomer, rather than purely vertical movement.
Gyrodus is the sole member of the pycnodont family Gyrodontidae, characterized by a depressed pit on the tooth occlusal surface and four dentary teeth.
It is classified in the Kingdom Animalia, Phylum Chordata, Class Actinopterygii, Order Pycnodontiformes, and Family Pycnodontidae.
The sister group to the Gyrodontidae family is thought to be the hypercarnivorous Serrasalmimidae, which previously included the genus Polygyrodus.
The type species of the genus Gyrodus is Gyrodus hexagonus.
Gyrodus was most abundant in Europe during the Late Jurassic and was also found off the coasts of East Asia and southern Americas.
Fossils became common during the Late Jurassic and are found throughout Europe, including France, Germany, Switzerland, Italy, and Spain.
In the Americas, remains are known from the Late Jurassic of Chile and the Kimmeridgian of Mexico.
In Asia, the fish is known from the Tithonian period in Japan and Siberia.
Indeterminate remains exist from the Early Cretaceous Barremian and Hauterivian of Germany, with the final known record being the species G. minor from the Aptian of England.
During the Late Jurassic, the distribution extended to many parts of the world, with some species also inhabiting the United States.
Species G. therfieldensis and G. menor are known from the Early Cretaceous.
The time range for Gyrodus spans from the Rhaetian to the Turonian, approximately 205.7 to 89.8 million years ago.
